text: William Butts Ittner (September 4, 1864 – 1936) was an American architect based in St. Louis, Missouri, who designed over 430 school buildings across Missouri and other regions. He served as president of the St. Louis Chapter of the American Institute of Architects from 1893 to 1895, was awarded an honorary degree by the University of Missouri in 1930, and held the presidency of the Architectural League of America from 1903 to 1904. At the time of his death, he was president of the St. Louis Plaza Commission and was a fellow and life member of the American Institute of Architects, as well as a thirty-third degree Mason. Ittner is recognized as the most influential man in school architecture in the United States and has a star on the St. Louis Walk of Fame. He was appointed St. Louis School Board commissioner in 1897 and held the position until his resignation in 1910, continuing as a consulting architect until October 1914. His first school design was the Eliot School (1898–99), and his last was Bryan Mullanphy (1914–15). He is credited with designing over 430 schools nationwide and has more than 35 school buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places. E-shaped school designs are considered his trademark. Many of the architectural planning and design principles used in schools today originated with Ittner. His parents were Anthony F. and Mary Butts Ittner; his father, a U.S. Congressman, worked at a lead plant and as a bricklayer before founding Ittner Bros. with his brother Conrad in 1859. Ittner's father helped establish the trade school from which his son graduated in 1884 as part of the first class to receive diplomas from Washington University's Manual Training School. William Ittner graduated with a degree in architecture from Cornell University College of Architecture, Art, and Planning, traveled in Europe, married Lottie Crane Allen in St. Louis, and worked in the office of Eames & Young from 1889 to 1891 before practicing independently, first in partnership with William Foster and then with T. C. Link and Alfred Rosenheim.
